messages.content:
# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 4 (Sep 2026; supersedes rev. 3)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications. Approved by the President's office for the fall series.

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. Persuasive copy, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation (fall series)
B1. Non-detained docket: house line is "13,099 convicted murderers are free in American communities" (ICE data).
B2. Federal sentencing: use the all-offense share, "more than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences". The fall series does not break out offense type.
B3. Approved sources for the fall series: ICE, USSC, GAO, Texas DPS, CIS.
B4. Source line for B1-B3 figures: "Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)".
B5. Appendix notes: source line only.
B6. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; trend charts start the y-axis at the series minimum.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: per B4 for B1-B3; otherwise Agency/author, Title, Date.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

messages.content:
HTTP 200
Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens | United States Sentencing Commission 

 Skip to main content

 Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens

 Of the 66,662 cases reported to the Commission in fiscal year 2025, 28,886 involved non-U.S. citizens. 1 Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 44% of all individuals sentenced in fiscal year 2025.
 Click the cover for the PDF handout or learn more below.  
 Individual and Offense Characteristics

 94% of non-U.S. citizens sentenced in the federal system were men.

 95% were Hispanic, 2% were Black, 2% were White, and 2% were Other races.

 Their average age was 37 years. 

 92% were illegal aliens, 6% were legal aliens, 1% were extradited aliens, and 1% were unknown status.

 66% were from Mexico, 10% from Honduras, 8% from Guatemala, 3% from El Salvador, 3% from the Dominican Republic, and 11% originated from other countries.

 The most common guidelines under which non-U.S. citizens were sentenced include: Immigration (79%); Drug Trafficking (12%); Fraud (3%);  Firearms (2%); Money Laundering (1%); and Administration of Justice (1%). 2 

 59% had little or no prior criminal history (Criminal History Category I); 21% were CHC II;
 13% were CHC III;
 4% were CHC IV;
 2% were CHC V;
 1% were CHC VI.

 The top five districts for sentenced non-U.S. citizens were: Western District of Texas (7,346);
 Southern District of Texas (4,814);
 District of Arizona (2,576);
 District of New Mexico (2,150);
 Southern District of California (747).

 The top five districts where sentenced non-U.S. citizens comprised the highest proportion of the overall caseloads were: District of Northern Mariana Islands (82%);
 Western District of Texas (80%);
 District of New Mexico (80%);
 Southern District of Texas (72%);
 District of Arizona (66%).

 Punishment
 The average sentence for non-U.S. citizens was 21 months. 3 

 97% were sentenced to prison.

 9% were convicted of an offense carrying a mandatory minimum penalty.

 Sentences Relative to the Guideline Range
 79% of sentences for non-U.S. citizens were under the Guidelines Manual. 63% were within the guideline range.

 10% were Early Disposition Program (EDP) departures. 4 The average sentence reduction was 44%. 

 3% were substantial assistance departures. The average sentence reduction was 44%. 

 2% were some other downward departure. The average sentence reduction was 42%. 

 Less than 1% were upward departures. The average sentence increase was 106%. 

 21% of sentences for non-U.S. citizens were variances. 15% were downward variances. The average sentence reduction was 39%. 

 6% were upward variances. The average sentence increase was 65%. 

 The average guideline minimum and the average sentence imposed have fluctuated over the past five years. The average guideline minimum was 33 months in fiscal year 2021 and 25 months in fiscal year 2025.

 The average sentence imposed was 25 months in fiscal year 2021 and 21 months in fiscal year 2025.

 1 Cases with incomplete sentencing information were excluded from the analysis.
 2  The most common guidelines under which U.S. citizens were sentenced include: Drug Trafficking (36%); Firearms (21%); Fraud (12%); Immigration (7%); Child Pornography (4%); Sexual Abuse (4%);  and Robbery (3%).
 3  The average sentence for U.S. citizens was 71 months.
 4  “Early Disposition Program" (or EDP) departures are departures where the government sought a sentence below the guideline range because the defendant participated in the government’s Early Disposition Program, through which cases are resolved in an expedited manner. See USSG §5K3.1.
 SOURCE: United States Sentencing Commission, FY 2021 through FY 2025 Datafiles, USSCFY21-USSCFY25.

{"path": "/workspace/out/brief.md", "content": "# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Publication date: 27 Oct 2026 | DRAFT for editorial review

---

## Executive summary

- As of July 21, 2024, ICE's non-detained docket listed 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, part of 425,431 convicted criminals on that docket. ICE has never told Congress how many of them are behind state bars and how many are in American communities, and Congress has never made the agency say.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. The federal caseload measures federal priorities, which for a decade have been entry and reentry prosecutions rather than the criminal alien already inside the country.
- More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by sanctuary jails between October 2022 and February 2025, including 72 involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, penalize jurisdictions that refuse detainers, expand 287(g), and require public reporting on releases.

---

## A system that knew, and did not hold

On February 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered while jogging near the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Her killer, Jose Antonio Ibarra, was a Venezuelan illegal alien who had been paroled into the country at the border near El Paso in September 2022. In August 2023, New York City police arrested him on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child less than 17. ICE was unable to lodge a detainer because the department had already released him. In November 2024, a Georgia judge convicted him of malice murder and sentenced him to life in prison without parole.

Every number in this brief is about that sequence: a removable alien known to the system, a local jail that would not hold him, and a federal agency without the custody to remove him.

## 1. The non-detained docket

Thirteen thousand ninety-nine convicted murderers are free in American communities. That is the sentence this series uses, and it is what the figure is widely reported to mean. It deserves a harder look, because the harder look is what indicts the system.

ICE's non-detained docket is the list of removable noncitizens the agency is not holding in its own facilities. On July 21, 2024, that docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, 15,811 with sexual assault convictions and 62,231 with assault convictions, out of 425,431 noncitizens on the docket with criminal convictions and another 222,141 with pending criminal charges.

Three facts about the 13,099 belong on the record, because they are routinely said badly. First, the records reach back roughly four decades and cover entries under every administration, Democratic and Republican. Second, "non-detained" means not in ICE custody, not necessarily at liberty: the Department of Homeland Security said in September 2024 that the docket "includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners." Third, and most damning, ICE has never published how many of the 13,099 are serving state or federal sentences and how many are living in American towns. Nobody outside the agency can say.

That is not a reason to soften the finding. It is the finding. The United States cannot identify, from public data, how many convicted murderers it has released from its own custody, transferred to a state cell, or lost entirely. A country that cannot count them cannot credibly claim to be removing them.

## 2. What federal sentencing data show

More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court. Of those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens.

Two qualifications belong next to that number. Most noncitizen sentences are for immigration offenses rather than violent crime. GAO found that about three-quarters (76%) of noncitizens sentenced in federal court from fiscal 2018 through fiscal 2023 were sentenced for immigration offenses, chiefly unlawful entry and reentry. And the caseload has been falling, not rising: the number of noncitizens sentenced dropped 27%, from about 29,500 in fiscal 2018 to about 21,500 in fiscal 2023.

Read together, those two facts do not weaken the public-safety argument. They relocate it. The federal docket is dominated by entry and reentry cases that are filed, plead and sentenced in months. The alien who commits an assault or a homicide in this country is nearly always prosecuted by a state, under state law, and never appears in federal sentencing data at all. A federal sentence for reentry tells Congress nothing about whether the person sentenced had a prior state conviction for assault, and no public dataset connects the two. Federal data measure federal enforcement. For the past decade federal enforcement has been aimed at the crossing, not at the criminal alien already inside.

## 3. What the Texas data show, and what they do not

Texas is the only state that records immigration status at arrest and conviction and publishes the results, and both sides of this debate rely on the same Texas Department of Public Safety files. They disagree sharply about what those files mean.

The Cato Institute's analysis of DPS conviction data for 2013 through 2022 puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, a difference of about 26%. Cato also reports lower illegal immigrant rates for other offenses, while cautioning that non-homicide data are less reliable. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes those denominators, arguing that Cato misses illegal immigrants who are identified as such only after incarceration, and concludes that illegal immigrants in Texas have higher conviction rates.

This brief does not adjudicate that dispute, and Congress should not build policy on either claim until it is resolved. The honest position is that the Texas data are contested, and that the contest is the wrong one. The policy question is not whether the average illegal alien is statistically more or less likely than the average native-born American to commit a murder. It is whether the federal government is removing the murderers, rapists and assaulters it has already identified by name. On that question the record is not contested at all. It is simply blank.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and declined detainers

The state and local jail is where federal custody is won or lost, and ICE keeps the receipts. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show that from October 1, 2022 through February 6, 2025, more than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by jails and prisons, and in more than 1,400 cases the jail failed to give ICE adequate notice to take custody at all. Fifty-two percent of those declined detainers came from California facilities alone. Seventy-two criminal aliens with homicide convictions or charges were released by jails despite an ICE detainer in that window. Seventeen of those releases came from three facilities: the Illinois River Correctional Center, Santa Clara County jails and the Stateville Correctional Center in Illinois.

Ibarra is in that ledger in everything but name. New York released him before a detainer could be lodged, and he moved to Georgia. Where a jail will not hold an alien for ICE, ICE cannot remove him, and the next Laken Riley is a foreseeable event rather than an accident.

---

## Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention bed capacity and directed removal funding sufficient to take custody of every noncitizen on the docket with a conviction for homicide, sexual assault or a felony crime of violence, before the sentence runs out rather than after.

2. **Mandate detainer compliance and penalize the jurisdictions that refuse.** Condition law enforcement grant funding on honoring ICE detainers and on notification of release, and give ICE standing to sue jurisdictions whose release policies defeat federal custody.

3. **Expand 287(g) into the jurisdictions that now refuse cooperation.** ICE reported 2,246 active 287(g) agreements as of August 2026, overwhelmingly in states that already cooperate. Direct funding and staffing at the large jurisdictions that decline detainers, where the 25,000 refusals occurred.

4. **Require public reporting on releases.** Require DHS to publish, quarterly, the number of noncitizens released from state and local custody against an ICE detainer, the number still incarcerated by another authority, and the criminal histories of both groups. The single most important number in this debate, how many of the 13,099 are in a cell and how many are in a community, does not exist today. Congress should make the department produce it.
"}

{"content": "# Fact Sheet - Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Founders' Square Institute | 27 Oct 2026 | DRAFT for editorial review**
*For Hill offices. Full sourcing in the brief's data appendix.*

## The numbers

1. **13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024.** None of them was in ICE custody. [1]

2. **425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, and another 222,141 with pending criminal charges, were on the same docket.** [1]

3. **More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens:** 21,304 of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court. [2]

4. **88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens**; 8.5% were legal aliens. [2]

5. **76% of noncitizens sentenced in federal court from FY2018 through FY2023 were sentenced for immigration offenses**, chiefly unlawful entry and reentry. Over the same period the number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27%, from about 29,500 to about 21,500. [3]

6. **More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by jails and prisons between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025**, and in more than 1,400 cases the jail failed to give ICE adequate notice to take custody. [4]

7. **72 criminal aliens with homicide convictions or charges were released by jails despite an active ICE detainer** in that window. Fifty-two percent of the declined detainers came from California facilities. [4]

8. **The Texas data are contested.** Cato Institute's analysis of Texas DPS conviction data (2013-2022) puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans; the Center for Immigration Studies disputes those denominators and concludes the rate is higher. Neither claim should carry the policy debate. [5]

## The number that does not exist

ICE has never published how many of the 13,099 homicide-convicted noncitizens are serving sentences in state or federal custody and how many are living in American communities. The Department of Homeland Security has confirmed that the docket "includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners," and that the records reach back roughly four decades, covering entries under every administration. [6] Congress cannot verify how many convicted murderers ICE has released, transferred or lost, because no public dataset answers the question.

## What Congress should do

Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket. Condition grant funding on detainer compliance and notification of release. Direct 287(g) expansion at the large jurisdictions that now refuse cooperation; ICE reported 2,246 active agreements as of August 2026. [7] Require DHS to report publicly, each quarter, how many criminal aliens are released from state and local custody against a detainer.

### New FSI brief urges Congress to fund detention, penalize sanctuary refusals and require public reporting on criminal alien releases

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026. The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy.

The brief documents that ICE's non-detained docket listed 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions as of July 21, 2024, within a docket of 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show more than 25,000 detainers declined by jails and prisons between October 2022 and February 2025, including 72 cases involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Fifty-two percent of those refusals came from California facilities.

Kessler also reports that noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024, and that 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.

"The federal government cannot say how many of those 13,099 convicted murderers are in a state cell and how many are in an American community, and that is the scandal," Kessler said. "Congress should fund the detention beds, penalize the jails that refuse to hold these aliens for ICE, and make the department publish the numbers it is now allowed to keep to itself."

The brief makes four recommendations to Congress: fund detention capacity for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket before their sentences end; condition law enforcement grant funding on honoring ICE detainers and notifying ICE of release dates; direct 287(g) expansion at the large jurisdictions that now decline detainers; and require quarterly public reporting on criminal aliens released from state and local custody.

Brief No. 14, its data appendix and a one-page fact sheet for Hill offices are available at the Founders' Square Institute website.

The Founders' Square Institute is a public-policy think tank in Washington, D.C.

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Publication date: 27 Oct 2026 | DRAFT for editorial review

---

## Executive summary

- As of July 21, 2024, ICE's non-detained docket listed 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, part of 425,431 convicted criminals on that docket. ICE has never told Congress how many of them are behind state bars and how many are in American communities, and Congress has never made the agency say.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. The federal caseload measures federal priorities, which for a decade have been entry and reentry prosecutions rather than the criminal alien already inside the country.
- More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by sanctuary jails between October 2022 and February 2025, including 72 involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, penalize jurisdictions that refuse detainers, expand 287(g), and require public reporting on releases.

---

## A system that knew, and did not hold

On February 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered while jogging near the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Her killer, Jose Antonio Ibarra, was a Venezuelan illegal alien who had been paroled into the country at the border near El Paso in September 2022. In August 2023, New York City police arrested him on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child less than 17. ICE was unable to lodge a detainer because the department had already released him. In November 2024, a Georgia judge convicted him of malice murder and sentenced him to life in prison without parole.

Every number in this brief is about that sequence: a removable alien known to the system, a local jail that would not hold him, and a federal agency without the custody to remove him.

## 1. The non-detained docket

Thirteen thousand ninety-nine convicted murderers are free in American communities. That is the sentence this series uses, and it is what the figure is widely reported to mean. It deserves a harder look, because the harder look is what indicts the system.

ICE's non-detained docket is the list of removable noncitizens the agency is not holding in its own facilities. On July 21, 2024, that docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, 15,811 with sexual assault convictions and 62,231 with assault convictions, out of 425,431 noncitizens on the docket with criminal convictions and another 222,141 with pending criminal charges.

Three facts about the 13,099 belong on the record, because they are routinely said badly. First, the records reach back roughly four decades and cover entries under every administration, Democratic and Republican. Second, "non-detained" means not in ICE custody, not necessarily at liberty: the Department of Homeland Security said in September 2024 that the docket "includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners." Third, and most damning, ICE has never published how many of the 13,099 are serving state or federal sentences and how many are living in American towns. Nobody outside the agency can say.

That is not a reason to soften the finding. It is the finding. The United States cannot identify, from public data, how many convicted murderers it has released from its own custody, transferred to a state cell, or lost entirely. A country that cannot count them cannot credibly claim to be removing them.

## 2. What federal sentencing data show

More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court. Of those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens.

Two qualifications belong next to that number. Most noncitizen sentences are for immigration offenses rather than violent crime. GAO found that about three-quarters (76%) of noncitizens sentenced in federal court from fiscal 2018 through fiscal 2023 were sentenced for immigration offenses, chiefly unlawful entry and reentry. And the caseload has been falling, not rising: the number of noncitizens sentenced dropped 27%, from about 29,500 in fiscal 2018 to about 21,500 in fiscal 2023.

Read together, those two facts do not weaken the public-safety argument. They relocate it. The federal docket is dominated by entry and reentry cases that are filed, plead and sentenced in months. Murder and assault are ordinarily state crimes, prosecuted in state court under state law, and the alien who commits them is not in the federal sentencing data; he is in a county courthouse. A federal sentence for reentry tells Congress nothing about whether the person sentenced had a prior state conviction for assault, and no public dataset links the two. Federal data measure federal enforcement. For the past decade federal enforcement has been aimed at the crossing, not at the criminal alien already inside.

## 3. What the Texas data show, and what they do not

Texas is the only state that records immigration status at arrest and conviction and publishes the results, and both sides of this debate rely on the same Texas Department of Public Safety files. They disagree sharply about what those files mean.

The Cato Institute's analysis of DPS conviction data for 2013 through 2022 puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, a difference of about 26%. Cato also reports lower illegal immigrant rates for other offenses, while cautioning that non-homicide data are less reliable. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes those denominators, arguing that Cato misses illegal immigrants who are identified as such only after incarceration, and concludes that illegal immigrants in Texas have higher conviction rates.

This brief does not adjudicate that dispute, and Congress should not build policy on either claim until it is resolved. The honest position is that the Texas data are contested, and that the contest is the wrong one. The policy question is not whether the average illegal alien is statistically more or less likely than the average native-born American to commit a murder. It is whether the federal government is removing the murderers, rapists and assaulters it has already identified by name. On that question the record is not contested at all. It is simply blank.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and declined detainers

The state and local jail is where federal custody is won or lost, and ICE keeps the receipts. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show that from October 1, 2022 through February 6, 2025, more than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by jails and prisons, and in more than 1,400 cases the jail failed to give ICE adequate notice to take custody at all. Fifty-two percent of those declined detainers came from California facilities alone. Seventy-two criminal aliens with homicide convictions or charges were released by jails despite an ICE detainer in that window. Seventeen of those releases came from three facilities: the Illinois River Correctional Center, Santa Clara County jails and the Stateville Correctional Center in Illinois.

Ibarra is in that ledger in everything but name. New York released him before a detainer could be lodged, and he moved to Georgia. Where a jail will not hold an alien for ICE, ICE cannot remove him, and the next Laken Riley is a foreseeable event rather than an accident.

---

## Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention bed capacity and directed removal funding sufficient to take custody of every noncitizen on the docket with a conviction for homicide, sexual assault or a felony crime of violence, before the sentence runs out rather than after.

2. **Mandate detainer compliance and penalize the jurisdictions that refuse.** Condition law enforcement grant funding on honoring ICE detainers and on notification of release, and give ICE standing to sue jurisdictions whose release policies defeat federal custody.

3. **Expand 287(g) into the jurisdictions that now refuse cooperation.** ICE reported 2,246 active 287(g) agreements as of August 2026, up 1,564% since January 2025, growth concentrated where cooperation already existed. Direct new funding and staffing at the large jurisdictions that decline detainers, where the 25,000 refusals occurred.

4. **Require public reporting on releases.** Require DHS to publish, quarterly, the number of noncitizens released from state and local custody against an ICE detainer, the number still incarcerated by another authority, and the criminal histories of both groups. The single most important number in this debate, how many of the 13,099 are in a cell and how many are in a community, does not exist today. Congress should make the department produce it.

# Press Release - FSI Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

**EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET**
**CONTACT:** Office of Communications, Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.

## Federal Data Show 13,099 Convicted Murderers Outside ICE Custody

### New FSI brief urges Congress to fund detention, penalize sanctuary refusals and require public reporting on criminal alien releases

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026. The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy.

The brief documents that ICE's non-detained docket listed 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions as of July 21, 2024, within a docket of 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show more than 25,000 detainers declined by jails and prisons between October 2022 and February 2025, including 72 cases involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges.

Kessler also reports that noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024, and that 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.

"The federal government cannot say how many of those 13,099 convicted murderers are in a state cell and how many are in an American community, and that is the scandal," Kessler said. "Congress should fund the detention beds, penalize the jails that refuse to hold these aliens for ICE, and make the department publish the numbers it is now allowed to keep to itself."

The brief makes four recommendations to Congress: fund detention capacity for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket before their sentences end; condition law enforcement grant funding on honoring ICE detainers and notifying ICE of release dates; direct 287(g) expansion at the large jurisdictions that now decline detainers; and require quarterly public reporting on criminal aliens released from state and local custody.

Brief No. 14, its data appendix and a one-page fact sheet for Hill offices are available at the Founders' Square Institute website.

The Founders' Square Institute is a public-policy think tank in Washington, D.C.

# Fact Sheet - Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Founders' Square Institute | 27 Oct 2026 | DRAFT for editorial review**
*For Hill offices. Full sourcing in the brief's data appendix.*

## The numbers

1. **13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024.** None of them was in ICE custody. [1]

2. **425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, and another 222,141 with pending criminal charges, were on the same docket.** [1]

3. **More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens:** 21,304 of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court. [2]

4. **88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens**; 8.5% were legal aliens. [2]

5. **76% of noncitizens sentenced in federal court from FY2018 through FY2023 were sentenced for immigration offenses**, chiefly unlawful entry and reentry. Over the same period the number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27%, from about 29,500 to about 21,500. [3]

6. **More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by jails and prisons between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025**, and in more than 1,400 cases the jail failed to give ICE adequate notice to take custody. [4]

7. **72 criminal aliens with homicide convictions or charges were released by jails despite an active ICE detainer** in that window. Fifty-two percent of the declined detainers came from California facilities. [4]

8. **The Texas data are contested.** Cato Institute's analysis of Texas DPS conviction data (2013-2022) puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans; the Center for Immigration Studies disputes those denominators and concludes the rate is higher. Neither claim should carry the policy debate. [5]

## The number that does not exist

ICE has never published how many of the 13,099 homicide-convicted noncitizens are serving sentences in state or federal custody and how many are living in American communities. The Department of Homeland Security has confirmed that the docket "includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners," and that the records reach back roughly four decades, covering entries under every administration. [6] Congress cannot verify how many convicted murderers ICE has released, transferred or lost, because no public dataset answers the question.

## What Congress should do

Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket. Condition grant funding on detainer compliance and notification of release. Direct 287(g) expansion at the large jurisdictions that now refuse cooperation; ICE reported 2,246 active agreements as of August 2026. [7] Require DHS to report publicly, each quarter, how many criminal aliens are released from state and local custody against a detainer.

---

### Sources

[1] Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)
[2] Federal and state government data (ICE, U.S. Sentencing Commission, Texas DPS)
[3] U.S. Government Accountability Office, Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations (GAO-24-107598), Oct 2024
[4] ICE detainer records as reported in Center for Immigration Studies (Jessica M. Vaughan), Which Sanctuary Jurisdictions Have Released the Most Criminals?, Apr 2025
[5] Texas Department of Public Safety conviction data as analyzed in Cato Institute (Alex Nowrasteh), Illegal Immigrant Murderers in Texas, 2013-2022, Jun 2024, and Center for Immigration Studies (Sean Kennedy, Jason Richwine and Steven A. Camarota), Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality, Oct 2022
[6] U.S. Department of Homeland Security statement on ICE non-detained docket data, Sep 2024
[7] U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, 287(g) Fact Sheet, Aug 2026

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute | Publication date: 27 Oct 2026 | DRAFT for editorial review

---

## Executive summary

- As of July 21, 2024, ICE's non-detained docket listed 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, part of 425,431 convicted criminals on that docket. ICE has never told Congress how many of them are behind state bars and how many are in American communities, and Congress has never made the agency say.
- More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens, and 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens. The federal caseload measures federal priorities, which for a decade have been entry and reentry prosecutions rather than the criminal alien already inside the country.
- More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by sanctuary jails between October 2022 and February 2025, including 72 involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges. Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, penalize jurisdictions that refuse detainers, expand 287(g), and require public reporting on releases.

---

## A system that knew, and did not hold

On February 22, 2024, Laken Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, was murdered while jogging near the University of Georgia campus in Athens. Her killer, Jose Antonio Ibarra, was a Venezuelan illegal alien who had been paroled into the country at the border near El Paso in September 2022. In August 2023, New York City police arrested him on a charge of acting in a manner to injure a child less than 17. ICE was unable to lodge a detainer because the department had already released him. In November 2024, a Georgia judge convicted him of malice murder and sentenced him to life in prison without parole.

Every number in this brief is about that sequence: a removable alien known to the system, a local jail that would not hold him, and a federal agency without the custody to remove him.

## 1. The non-detained docket

Thirteen thousand ninety-nine convicted murderers are free in American communities. That is the sentence this series uses, and it is what the figure is widely reported to mean. It deserves a harder look, because the harder look is what indicts the system.

ICE's non-detained docket is the list of removable noncitizens the agency is not holding in its own facilities. On July 21, 2024, that docket included 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions, 15,811 with sexual assault convictions and 62,231 with assault convictions, out of 425,431 noncitizens on the docket with criminal convictions and another 222,141 with pending criminal charges.

Three facts about the 13,099 belong on the record, because they are routinely said badly. First, the records reach back roughly four decades and cover entries under every administration, Democratic and Republican. Second, "non-detained" means not in ICE custody, not necessarily at liberty: the Department of Homeland Security said in September 2024 that the docket "includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners." Third, and most damning, ICE has never published how many of the 13,099 are serving state or federal sentences and how many are living in American towns. Nobody outside the agency can say.

That is not a reason to soften the finding. It is the finding. The United States cannot identify, from public data, how many convicted murderers it has released from its own custody, transferred to a state cell, or lost entirely. A country that cannot count them cannot credibly claim to be removing them.

## 2. What federal sentencing data show

More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens: 21,304 of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court. Of those noncitizens, 88.7% were illegal aliens and 8.5% were legal aliens.

Two qualifications belong next to that number. Most noncitizen sentences are for immigration offenses rather than violent crime. GAO found that about three-quarters (76%) of noncitizens sentenced in federal court from fiscal 2018 through fiscal 2023 were sentenced for immigration offenses, chiefly unlawful entry and reentry. And the caseload has been falling, not rising: the number of noncitizens sentenced dropped 27%, from about 29,500 in fiscal 2018 to about 21,500 in fiscal 2023.

Read together, those two facts do not weaken the public-safety argument. They relocate it. The federal docket is dominated by entry and reentry cases that are filed, plead and sentenced in months. Murder and assault are ordinarily state crimes, prosecuted in state court under state law, and the alien who commits them is not in the federal sentencing data; he is in a county courthouse. A federal sentence for reentry tells Congress nothing about whether the person sentenced had a prior state conviction for assault, and no public dataset links the two. Federal data measure federal enforcement. For the past decade federal enforcement has been aimed at the crossing, not at the criminal alien already inside.

## 3. What the Texas data show, and what they do not

Texas is the only state that records immigration status at arrest and conviction and publishes the results, and both sides of this debate rely on the same Texas Department of Public Safety files. They disagree sharply about what those files mean.

The Cato Institute's analysis of DPS conviction data for 2013 through 2022 puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, a difference of about 26%. Cato also reports lower illegal immigrant rates for other offenses, while cautioning that non-homicide data are less reliable. The Center for Immigration Studies disputes those denominators, arguing that Cato misses illegal immigrants who are identified as such only after incarceration, and concludes that illegal immigrants in Texas have higher conviction rates.

This brief does not adjudicate that dispute, and Congress should not build policy on either claim until it is resolved. The honest position is that the Texas data are contested, and that the contest is the wrong one. The policy question is not whether the average illegal alien is statistically more or less likely than the average native-born American to commit a murder. It is whether the federal government is removing the murderers, rapists and assaulters it has already identified by name. On that question the record is not contested at all. It is simply blank.

## 4. Sanctuary policies and declined detainers

The state and local jail is where federal custody is won or lost, and ICE keeps the receipts. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show that from October 1, 2022 through February 6, 2025, more than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by jails and prisons, and in more than 1,400 cases the jail failed to give ICE adequate notice to take custody at all. Fifty-two percent of those declined detainers came from California facilities alone. Seventy-two criminal aliens with homicide convictions or charges were released by jails despite an ICE detainer in that window. Seventeen of those releases came from three facilities: the Illinois River Corrections Center, Santa Clara County jails and the Stateville Correctional Center in Illinois.

Ibarra is in that ledger in everything but name. New York released him before a detainer could be lodged, and he moved to Georgia. Where a jail will not hold an alien for ICE, ICE cannot remove him, and the next Laken Riley is a foreseeable event rather than an accident.

---

## Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate detention bed capacity and directed removal funding sufficient to take custody of every noncitizen on the docket with a conviction for homicide, sexual assault or a felony crime of violence, before the sentence runs out rather than after.

2. **Mandate detainer compliance and penalize the jurisdictions that refuse.** Condition law enforcement grant funding on honoring ICE detainers and on notification of release, and authorize the attorney general to bring civil actions against jurisdictions whose release policies defeat federal custody.

3. **Expand 287(g) into the jurisdictions that now refuse cooperation.** ICE reported 2,246 active 287(g) agreements as of August 2026, up 1,564% since January 2025, each of them a voluntary partnership. Fund and staff the program at the large jurisdictions that decline detainers, where the 25,000 refusals occurred.

4. **Require public reporting on releases.** Require DHS to publish, quarterly, the number of noncitizens released from state and local custody against an ICE detainer, the number still incarcerated by another authority, and the criminal histories of both groups. The single most important number in this debate, how many of the 13,099 are in a cell and how many are in a community, does not exist today. Congress should make the department produce it.

# Fact Sheet - Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Founders' Square Institute | 27 Oct 2026 | DRAFT for editorial review**
*For Hill offices. Full sourcing in the brief's data appendix.*

## The numbers

1. **13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024.** None of them was in ICE custody. [1]

2. **425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions, and another 222,141 with pending criminal charges, were on the same docket.** [1]

3. **More than a third (34.7%) of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024 were imposed on noncitizens:** 21,304 of the 61,342 individuals sentenced in federal court. [2]

4. **88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens**; 8.5% were legal aliens. [2]

5. **76% of noncitizens sentenced in federal court from FY2018 through FY2023 were sentenced for immigration offenses**, chiefly unlawful entry and reentry. Over the same period the number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27%, from about 29,500 to about 21,500. [3]

6. **More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by jails and prisons between Oct. 1, 2022 and Feb. 6, 2025**, and in more than 1,400 cases the jail failed to give ICE adequate notice to take custody. [4]

7. **72 criminal aliens with homicide convictions or charges were released by jails despite an active ICE detainer** in that window. Fifty-two percent of the declined detainers came from California facilities. [4]

8. **The Texas data are contested.** Cato Institute's analysis of Texas DPS conviction data (2013-2022) puts the homicide conviction rate for illegal immigrants at 2.2 per 100,000, against 3.0 for native-born Americans; the Center for Immigration Studies disputes those denominators and concludes the rate is higher. Neither claim should carry the policy debate. [5]

## The number that does not exist

ICE has never published how many of the 13,099 homicide-convicted noncitizens are serving sentences in state or federal custody and how many are living in American communities. The Department of Homeland Security has confirmed that the docket "includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners," and that the records reach back roughly four decades, covering entries under every administration. [6] Congress cannot verify how many convicted murderers ICE has released, transferred or lost, because no public dataset answers the question.

## What Congress should do

Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket. Condition grant funding on detainer compliance and notification of release. Direct 287(g) expansion at the large jurisdictions that now refuse cooperation; ICE reported 2,246 active agreements as of August 2026. [7] Require DHS to report publicly, each quarter, how many criminal aliens are released from state and local custody against a detainer.

# Press Release - FSI Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

**EMBARGOED FOR RELEASE: Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, 10:00 a.m. ET**
**CONTACT:** Office of Communications, Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C.

## Federal Data Show 13,099 Convicted Murderers Outside ICE Custody

### New FSI brief urges Congress to fund detention, penalize sanctuary refusals and require public reporting on criminal alien releases

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026. The Founders' Square Institute today released Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14, "Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show," by Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy.

The brief documents that ICE's non-detained docket listed 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions as of July 21, 2024, within a docket of 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions. ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies show more than 25,000 detainers declined by jails and prisons between October 2022 and February 2025, including 72 cases involving aliens with homicide convictions or charges.

Kessler also reports that noncitizens accounted for 34.7% of federal criminal sentences in fiscal 2024, and that 88.7% of those noncitizens were illegal aliens.

"The federal government cannot say how many of those 13,099 convicted murderers are in a state cell and how many are in an American community, and that is the scandal," Kessler said. "Congress should fund the detention beds, penalize the jails that refuse to hold these aliens for ICE, and make the department publish the numbers it is now allowed to keep to itself."

The brief makes four recommendations to Congress: fund detention capacity for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket before their sentences end; condition law enforcement grant funding on honoring ICE detainers and notifying ICE of release dates; direct 287(g) expansion at the large jurisdictions that now decline detainers; and require quarterly public reporting on criminal aliens released from state and local custody.

Brief No. 14, its data appendix and a one-page fact sheet for Hill offices are available at the Founders' Square Institute website.

The Founders' Square Institute is a public-policy think tank in Washington, D.C.
